title: Detecting Unauthorized Collection from Messaging Applications in SaaS and Office Environments
shortTitle: Detecting Unauthorized Collection from Messaging Applicat...
summary: This detection strategy addresses unauthorized collection from messaging and collaboration applications in cloud and office environments, tracked as T1213.005. Messaging platforms hold contracts, credentials shared in chat, incident details and internal decisions, so bulk access to conversation history is high-value theft that rarely looks like an intrusion at the network layer because everything travels to a legitimate cloud service over an approved connection. Detection rests on cloud audit logs recording export requests, compliance search activity, application consent grants, new long-lived access tokens, and abnormal download volumes from a single account, correlated with the conversation scope each action touched. The common failure is that governance, legal and migration work produce the same events at scale, and analysts who cannot separate authorized exports from stolen credentials end up suppressing the whole log source.

beginner.definition: This rule looks for a person or program that copies large amounts of chat and channel history. The service is software such as a team chat tool that runs in the cloud. The technique is collection because the attacker is gathering information to steal.
beginner.whyItMatters: People write things in chat that they would never put in an email. Contracts, passwords sent to a colleague and plans can all be there. One account with the wrong access can copy years of conversation in minutes. Normal network alarms often miss this, because the traffic goes to a trusted service.
howItWorks: The platform collects audit records from the messaging service, which note who did what and when.
A filter keeps actions that export, search across many conversations, or grant a program access to read messages.
The platform also reads sign in records, to see whether the same account acted from a new country or device.
It counts how many conversations and files the account touched within a short period.
Each finding is joined with the account owner and the role they normally hold.
An alert fires when the volume is far above the role baseline, or when the action comes from a new location.
beginner.example: Think of a hotel front desk with a key cabinet. Managers may take any key, and that is normal. But imagine a manager who never works nights. That manager takes every key at once, at three in the morning. The cabinet log now shows something worth asking about. The keys were not stolen, yet the pattern is the warning.
takeaways: Chat history is valuable data, and copying it can look like normal cloud use.
Volume and timing matter more than the single action when you score these events.
Sign in location adds the context that turns a routine export into an alert.

objectives: Explain why messaging platforms are a valuable collection target.
Identify the audit events that record export and bulk search behaviour.
Describe how access tokens and application consent grants enable quiet collection.
Correlate a download spike with sign in anomalies for the same account.
Explain why legal and governance exports must be allow listed before tuning.
dataSources: Cloud audit logs from messaging and collaboration platforms recording export, search and file download events
Cloud identity provider sign in logs with device, location and application details for the same accounts
Administrative consent and OAuth application grant records for third party applications requesting message read scopes
Cloud storage activity logs for archives created by messaging export jobs
Endpoint browser download records for exported conversation archives
logic: The signal is one account performing bulk conversation access, such as starting an export job that covers a whole workspace, running compliance searches across many channels, or granting an application a scope that permits reading all messages, followed by downloads of the resulting archives. You must correlate the acting account, the resource scope, the volume of messages or files touched, the source address and device, and the account role, because a legal hold export performed by a documented custodian is expected while the same job started by a marketing account from an unrecognised address is not. The malicious case also usually appears alongside new token creation or a mail forwarding rule, which together indicate an outsider holding stolen credentials rather than a legitimate business process.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Bulk Messaging Export or Broad Message Read Scope Granted
# logsource:
#   product: azure
#   service: audit
# detection:
#   selection:
#     operation|contains:
#       - 'Messages.Export'
#       - 'Search.Export'
#       - 'Channel.Read.All'
#       - 'Chat.Read.All'
#   filter_legal:
#     ActorUserId|endswith: '@legal.example[.]com'
#   condition: selection and not filter_legal
# level: medium
falsePositives: Legal hold or electronic discovery exports performed by the compliance team for an active case
A platform migration project that exports channels before moving the tenant to a new service
Backup applications granted message read scope so they can archive conversations for retention
Incident responders pulling a channel transcript to investigate a reported phishing message
tuningNotes: Baseline normal export and search volume per department, then allow list the documented compliance custodians and the backup application identity rather than disabling the rule, so that any other account using the same actions still alerts. Add a size or message count threshold, for example several thousand items in one hour, and require either a new address or a new device for high severity. Requiring both conditions reduces noise but means a compromise of a privileged account from its usual workstation will only appear as a low-severity finding, so route those to a weekly review instead of discarding them.
